claims.text: The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the selected equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after standardized thermomechanical processing.
Constituent count alone is inadequate to explain differences in deformation and failure behavior among these alloys.
Specific combinations of alloying elements produce different degrees of local lattice distortion.
Changes in local lattice distortion modulate stacking fault energy.
Variations in stacking fault energy alter dislocation mobility.
Variations in stacking fault energy alter the balance between slip and twinning during deformation.
The full ensemble of elements in the quinary alloy produces a uniquely balanced stacking fault energy.
The stacking fault energy of the quinary alloy slows dislocation motion.
The stacking fault energy of the quinary alloy promotes deformation mechanisms such as twinning or cross-slip.
The promoted deformation mechanisms enhance strain hardening in the quinary alloy.
Quaternary and ternary subsets lack element pairs or triads needed to achieve the proposed optimized stacking fault energy.
The proposed nonoptimal stacking fault energies of the subsets lead to earlier plastic instability.
Relative to the quinary alloy, the quaternary alloys will exhibit lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary alloy, the ternary alloys will exhibit especially low strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary alloy, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit lower yield strength.
Relative to the quinary alloy, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit reduced ductility.
The proposed relationships apply under identical thermomechanical histories and room-temperature tensile testing at constant strain rate in ambient atmosphere.
